summary: Friedrich Gottlieb Welcker worked in history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at the University of Giessen (c. 1801–1803) and later held posts at Giessen (c. 1808–1816), Göttingen (c. 1816–1819), and Bonn (c. 1819–1861).

Haag studied at Zurich under Heinrich Schweizer-Sidler, as well as Göttingen and Berlin. He taught at Zurich, Tallinn, Schaffhausen, and Burgdorf before holding professorships in classical philology at the University of Bern (1887, 1891–1906).

Friedrich Heiler worked in religious studies. After completing his dissertation at the University of Munich (c. 1912–1917) and teaching there in 1918, he was appointed at the University of Marburg (1920) and directed the Religionskundliche Sammlung (c. 1927–1962).

Friedrich Hirth worked in Sinology, history, and archaeology. He studied at Leipzig, Berlin, and Greifswald, served in the Chinese Maritime Customs Service (1870–1897), and held the Dean Lung Professorship of Chinese at Columbia University (1902).
Friedrich Kurschat worked in linguistics. He studied at the University of Königsberg from c. 1836 to 1844 and held a post there from c. 1841 to 1883.

Friedrich Leo worked in linguistics and related fields. He studied at Göttingen and Bonn under Hermann Usener, later holding posts at Bonn, Kiel, Rostock, Strasbourg, and the University of Göttingen (1889–1914).

Friedrich Majer worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. He studied at the University of Jena (c. 1789–1792) and under Johann Gottfried von Herder (c. 1795–1803), serving as a Privatdozent at Jena (c. 1800–1802).

Max Müller worked in Indology, religious studies, and linguistics. He studied at Leipzig, Berlin, and Paris under Brockhaus, Bopp, Schelling, and Burnouf, and under H. H. Wilson. He spent his career at Oxford from 1850 to 1900.

Friedrich Müller worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at Vienna, Göttingen, and Tübingen under Anton Boller, later serving as Privatdozent (1858–1866) and Professor (from 1869) at the University of Vienna.
Friedrich Nietzsche worked in philosophy and linguistics. He studied at Bonn and Leipzig under Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl, and served as a faculty member at the University of Basel from 1869 to 1878.

Friedrich Otto Schrader worked in Indology and philosophy. He studied at the University of Strasbourg (c. 1899–1902), directed the Adyar Library and Research Centre (1905–1916), and became a professor at Kiel University in 1921.
Friedrich Ottomar Eduard Wilhelm held academic posts at the University of Freiburg (c. 1920–1922) and the University of Munich.
Friedrich Rosen studied under Franz Bopp from c. 1824 to 1826 and served as Professor of Sanskrit at the University of London from c. 1828 to 1837.

Friedrich Rückert worked in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied at Würzburg, Heidelberg, and under Bopp and Hammer-Purgstall, later holding professorships at Erlangen-Nuremberg (1826) and Berlin (1841–1849).

Schlegel worked in Indology, linguistics, and philosophy. He studied at Göttingen and Leipzig, and under Heyne, Hamilton, and Chézy. He held posts at Jena (1800), Cologne (1804), and TU Dresden (1828).

Friedrich Schleiermacher worked in philosophy and religious studies. He studied at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (c. 1787–1790) and held posts at Halle-Wittenberg (c. 1804–1807) and Humboldt University of Berlin (c. 1810–1834).
Friedrich Schrader worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. He completed his dissertation under Richard Pischel at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg between c. 1885 and 1889.

Friedrich Weller worked in Indology, Sinology, and Buddhist studies. He studied under August Conrady at Leipzig, where he subsequently served as Privatdozent (c. 1922–1928) and held the chair of Indian philology (1938–1958).

Friedrich Wilhelm works in Indology and Tibetology. He studied at Munich under Paul Thieme and served at the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Munich (Privatdozent 1963, Professor 1969–1998), with visiting professorships at Columbia and Collège de France.
Friedrich Wilhelm Graf worked in religious studies and related fields, holding academic posts at the University of Augsburg (c. 1992–1999) and the University of Munich (c. 1999–2014).
